items.text: Design named with a common term in title or abstract.
Abstract gives a balanced summary of methods and findings.
Why the study was needed: background and rationale.
Specific aims and any hypotheses fixed in advance.
Design stated early in the methods.
Where and when: site, recruitment period, exposure, follow-up, data collection.
Who was eligible, how selected, and how followed up.
Matching, sampling or follow-up details, as the design requires.
Operational definitions of outcome, exposure, confounders, effect modifiers and diagnoses.
Data source and measurement for each variable; comparability across groups.
Steps taken against likely sources of bias.
Justification of the sample size.
Treatment of quantitative variables, and reasons for any groupings.
Every statistical method, including confounding control.
Methods for subgroup and interaction analyses.
Approach to missing data.
How loss to follow-up or non-response was handled, per design.
Any sensitivity analyses.
Participant numbers at each stage, from eligible to analysed.
Why participants dropped out at each stage.
A participant flow diagram, if useful.
Participant characteristics, exposures and potential confounders.
Count of missing values per variable of interest.
Follow-up duration or time at risk, where the design has it.
Outcome counts or summary measures, suited to the design.
Crude and adjusted estimates with CIs; which confounders and why.
Cut-points used when continuous variables were grouped.
Absolute risk translation of relative estimates, where meaningful.
Results of other analyses: subgroups, interactions, sensitivity.
Main findings related back to the objectives.
Limitations: bias and imprecision, with likely direction and size.
Cautious overall reading given limitations, multiplicity and outside evidence.
Whether results apply beyond the study population (external validity).
Who funded the study and what the funder did.
